summary: Nez Perce National Forest cupola cabin on North Pole, built 1927 (D-6) and abandoned in 1950; a 2020 climbing guide says only the foundation remains.

facts.status_note: Abandoned in 1950 and destroyed at a later date; the 2020 climbing guide says only the foundation remains.

access.note: Hike to the peak on a trail in the Gospel Hump Wilderness; the climbing guide says it is easily reached by trail. No closure appears in the sources read.

visit.trail_note: About 2.5 miles and 1,225 ft of gain from Wildhorse Campground; trail not frequently maintained but in fair condition (2020 guide).

events.note: Cupola cabin; D-6 design per Forest Lookouts (Kresek)
Decommissioned in 1950 per the climbing guide

evidence.quote: This cupola cabin, built in 1927, was abandoned in 1950.
The site is located in the Gospel Hump Wilderness.

evidence.supports: about 17 miles southwest of Elk City
fire lookout established on the peak in 1927
evidence.quote: A fire lookout was established on the peak in 1927.

evidence.supports: decommissioned in 1950, destroyed at a later date
evidence.quote: The lookout was decommissioned in 1950 and destroyed at a later date.

evidence.supports: location in the Gospel Hump Wilderness
evidence.quote: North Pole is located roughly 17 miles SW of Elk City in the Gospel Hump Wilderness.

evidence.supports: 2.5-mile hike from Wildhorse Campground with 1,225 ft of gain
evidence.quote: It is 2.5 miles with 1,225 feet of elevation gain from Wildhorse Campground to the summit.
Unlike its slightly taller neighbor, Buffalo Hump, it is easily reached by trail.
The trail is not frequently maintained but is still in fair condition.

evidence.supports: remains of an old lookout and a pile of rocks; no summit register
evidence.quote: There is no summit register, only the remains of an old lookout and a pile of rocks.

notes_for_editor: The 1927 and 1950 dates agree across five pages, and two independent sites (climbing guide and SummitPost) describe what is left on the summit, though both are secondary and the guide is from 2020. No source gives the year the lookout was destroyed, so no destruction event is recorded. The record's material 'wood' (from design) does not appear in any page I read, so it is not written up; the D-6 design comes from Forest Lookouts, which cites Ray Kresek. A search snippet linked a cupola cabin with different dates to another lookout; it was not used. Staffing: idahofirelookouts.com says none is documented, so staffing is left out. Access level 'public' is inferred from the wilderness trail description; no closure was found. The existing record photo (idahofirelookouts.com, 1927) is kept; no new photos were found.
